first_draft.title: Alice, Bob, and the Dim Little Star
first_draft.text:
Alice lived in a yellow house at the end of Pebble Lane. Her best friend was a ginger cat named Bob, who had a crooked tail, a purr like a teakettle, and whiskers that could sniff out a sunbeam from across the room.

One evening, Alice climbed onto the windowsill with Bob tucked under her arm. "Look, Bob," she whispered. "The little star above the apple tree is dim." Bob blinked his slow cat blink. Every night that star twinkled like a silver button. Tonight it looked fuzzy, as if someone had breathed on it.

Bob's ears swiveled toward the glass. "Mrrp?" he said, which in cat means, Tell me more.

Then a moth fluttered out of the dark and bumped against the window. Thump. Flutter. Thump. It was a plump little moth with dusty gray wings and a furry body, and it would not stop knocking.

The moth flew down to a corner of the glass and landed on a shiny smudge. Alice pressed her nose close. The smudge was sticky, and it was shaped like a small handprint, right in front of the star.

Alice giggled. "Somebody had jammy fingers," she said. "I bet it was Sam."

Alice rubbed the smudge with her sleeve. Squeak, squish. It smeared into a long, wobbly streak, and the star looked even dimmer. Bob patted at the glass with one paw, then sat back and shook his foot. "Mrrrp!" His paw was sticky now, too, and he gave it a look of great disgust.

The moth bumped the glass again, softly, as if to say, Slow down. Alice took a deep breath. "Grandma knows all about smudges," she whispered, and she tiptoed down the hall in her socks.

Grandma was knitting by the fire with her glasses on her nose. When she heard the story, she smiled and fetched a bowl of warm water and a soft cloth. "Small circles, not big rubs," she said. "Smudges like gentle hands."

Alice dipped the cloth and began wiping in tiny circles. Round and round, soft as a whisper. Bob sat on the sill and watched every circle with his tail wrapped around his feet. The moth landed on Alice's knuckle and stayed there, as still as a button.

Little by little, the sticky smudge loosened and slid away. Alice rinsed the cloth and wiped one last time. The glass was clear and cool under her fingers.

Above the apple tree, the little star blinked. Then it glowed, bright and silver, like it had just woken from a nap.

"We did it!" Alice gasped. Bob gave a proud little chirrup and flicked his crooked tail. The moth lifted off Alice's hand and circled the star once, twice, before it drifted away into the cool night.

Grandma tucked the cloth away and yawned a big, slow yawn. Alice climbed into bed, and Bob curled up on her pillow, purring softer and softer. The star twinkled, slow and sleepy now. Its light crept across the floor and over the quilt, warm as honey.

"Goodnight, little star," Alice whispered.

Bob's purr hummed like a teakettle at rest.

Goodnight, Bob. Goodnight, moth.

The room grew quiet. Then very quiet. And then the whole house was still.

request: Leo and his dog Rocket go on a treasure hunt in the backyard

first_draft.title: Rocket and the Backyard Treasure
first_draft.text:
Leo found the map under his pillow on a rainy Saturday morning. It was rolled up tight and tied with a piece of green yarn, and it smelled like old paper and dried mint. Someone had drawn a big red X beside the old oak tree in the backyard.

"Rocket! Ahoy, matey!" Leo shouted, waving the map over his head. His dog, a scruffy brown terrier with one floppy ear, spun in a circle and barked. Woof! Woof-woof! Rocket was ready for an adventure.

Leo tucked the map into his pocket and grabbed his toy spyglass. The two of them tiptoed down the back steps, past the wet flower pots and the squeaky gate. The grass was cold and damp under their feet. Splish, splash, squish! Rocket sniffed every single blade of grass as if it held a secret.

The map said to walk ten giant steps from the oak tree. Leo counted out loud. "One, two, three..." At seven, his sneaker slipped on a muddy patch. He landed on his bottom with a plop. Rocket licked his nose, and Leo giggled so hard he got the hiccups. Hic! Hic! "Ten," he finished, wiping his face. "We're almost there, Rocket."

But when Leo looked down, there was only a pile of soggy leaves. No chest. No gold. Leo frowned and scratched his head. Rocket began digging, paws flying, dirt spraying everywhere. Leo laughed and joined in, pulling away sticks and leaves with both hands.

Then Rocket stopped. He sat very still and wagged his tail, slowly, like a clock ticking. Leo knelt down. Underneath the leaves was a small wooden box, painted with blue waves. Its lid had a tiny brass latch.

"Ready, Rocket?" Leo whispered. He lifted the latch. Click!

Inside, nestled on a folded napkin, was a shiny blue marble, a silver button, and a note in careful handwriting. The note said, "For the finder of the treasure: Every adventure ends with a friend." Beneath it was a dog biscuit shaped like a star.

Leo grinned from ear to ear. Rocket gobbled the biscuit in one happy crunch. "Our best treasure was the digging," Leo said, and Rocket wagged his whole back end.

They walked slowly back up the steps. Leo tucked the marble in his pocket, next to the map. The rain had stopped. The sky turned soft and gray, then pink, then purple. Somewhere a bird sang one last sleepy song.

Inside, Leo's mom was waiting with warm toast and a towel. She wrapped him up tight. Rocket curled into his blanket with a long, contented sigh.

Leo yawned. His eyes grew heavy. The marble glowed softly on the nightstand.

Good night, Rocket. Good night, treasure.

Shh now. The house is quiet, and the stars are coming out, one by one.

Inside, Leo's mom was waiting with warm cinnamon toast and a fluffy towel. She wrapped him up tight. Rocket shook his wet fur and curled into his blanket with a long, contented sigh.

Leo yawned. His eyes grew heavy. The marble glowed softly on the nightstand.

first_draft.title: Ember and the Dandelion Wind
first_draft.text:
On top of Lantern Hill, a little dragon named Ember sat very still. The sun was sinking behind the far green hills. Her wings were folded tight, like two wet umbrellas.

Below her, in a mossy hollow, lived her friend Old Mossy. He was a tortoise, and he was never in a hurry. Scritch, scratch. Scritch, scratch. He climbed up the hill one slow step at a time.

"Good evening, Ember," he said. "Why so quiet?"

"The sky is too big," whispered Ember. "And I am too small. I am scared of flying."

Old Mossy nodded. He did not laugh. He sat down beside her and looked at the sky too.

Ember stood on the edge of the rock. She puffed out her chest. She flapped her wings. "Flap, flap, flap!" Whoosh went the wind. Splat went Ember, right into a patch of purple clover.

"Only my pride," grumbled Ember. A little puff of sparkles drifted out of her nose.

first_draft.title: Clementine and the Midnight Crisper Party
first_draft.text:
At midnight, when the kitchen went dark and the fridge hummed its sleepy hum, the vegetables began to wiggle.

Clementine the carrot hopped out of the crisper drawer with a crunchy little bounce. "Party time!" she whispered. The green beans went zip, zip, zip. A cucumber went whoosh, whoosh. A row of radishes went pop, pop, pop, like tiny bubbles in lemonade.

The party was on the middle shelf, glowing in the cool light. Lettuce leaves made a fancy green tablecloth. Cherry tomatoes bobbed like red balloons. A bowl of peas rattled like a tambourine, and everybody tapped their toes.

Clementine counted the guests. One, two, three, all the way to twelve. Then she stopped counting.

"Where is Milo?"

Everyone looked up at the door shelf. There, tucked behind a jar of pickles, stood a tall milk carton. His cap was screwed on tight, and his side said MILK in faded letters. He had not moved all evening.

"Milo!" called Clementine. "Come to the party!"

The carton gave a sad little slosh. "No, thank you," he said. "I am too tall and too square. I can't wiggle. I only know how to stand still."

"Then we will come to you!" said Clementine.

The green beans tried first. They wound up the side of the fridge door, zip, zip, zip, but they tangled into a knot and giggled so hard they fell right back down. Ha-ha-hoo!

The tomatoes tried next. They bounced up, boing, boing, boing, and bonked against the pickle jar. Bonk! Bonk! Bonk! The pickles rocked, and the jar rocked, and everyone had to hold their leaves over their ears to keep from laughing.

"Our leaves are too little," sighed a radish. "And the shelf is too high."

Clementine stared at the lettuce tablecloth, long and soft and frilly at the edges. An idea went tingle, tingle down her orange stem.

"Lettuce!" she cried. "Lay your leaves down like a slide!"

The lettuce leaves stretched out, one after another, from the door shelf all the way to the middle shelf, a long green ramp rustling like a whisper of wind.

Milo looked at the slide. He looked at his friends waving up at him, and at the cucumber doing a little happy hop. His cap wobbled. "Are you sure you want a carton at your party?"

"Yes!" shouted all twelve guests at once.

Milo took a deep breath. Slosh, slosh, slosh. Down he came, sliding and swooshing, whoosh, whoosh, whoosh, until he landed right in the middle of the party with a soft, cheerful thump.

The whole party cheered. The peas rattled. The beans zipped. The radishes popped. And Milo, who had only ever stood still, found himself swaying side to side, slosh, slosh, slosh, right in the dance.

Slowly, the dancing grew softer. The peas stopped rattling. The beans curled up in a sleepy bunch. Milo leaned against Clementine, cool and gentle. The lettuce tablecloth was folded as neat as a blanket. The fridge light dimmed, click, and the kitchen went still.

"Shh," whispered Clementine. "Goodnight, cucumbers. Goodnight, radishes. Goodnight, Milo."

"Goodnight," hummed the fridge, softly, softly, hmmmm.

Oona the owl was perched on her favorite branch, blinking sleepily. "A missing star?" she hooted. "Stars do not wander off by themselves, you know." She ruffled her feathers. "But I did see a glimmer near the pond, past the tall reeds."

Through the whispering grass they went, Figgy puffing and Oona gliding. Tobin the tortoise was already at the pond's edge, looking very pleased with himself. "Hello, Figgy," he said slowly. "I got here first. It only took me all evening." He pointed one wrinkly foot. Out over the water, a faint silver light dangled from a sticky web strung between the reeds.

Oona tried to snatch the star with her talons, but the threads stuck to her feathers. "Sticky, sticky, sticky!" she squeaked, shaking her wings until a bit of web floated off like a silver snowflake. Tobin tried pushing a reed aside, but he was so slow that the reed sprang back and gave him a gentle bonk on the head. "Ow," said Tobin, looking surprised. Then he began to giggle.

Figgy sat in his puddle and thought. He studied the web one thread at a time. "Oona," he said, "could you hold this strand very still, like a little bridge? Figgy curled into a round, prickly ball on a bed of soft leaves, and the wind hummed a lullaby through the grass. The moon grew thin and sleepy. Shh, the stars are watching. first_draft.title: The Yarn That Went Missing
first_draft.text:
Mabel the hen woke up grumpy. Her feathers were ruffled. "Cluck, cluck, grumble-bumble," she said.

Biscuit the puppy woke up bouncy. His tail wagged so hard. "Morning, Mabel! Morning, barn! Morning, muddy puddle!" SPLOOSH! He jumped right into the puddle.

"Grumble-bumble," said Mabel. "Biscuit, you are soggy."

"I am a very soggy puppy!" said Biscuit happily. "Want to play?"

"No," said Mabel. "I want my yellow yarn. I was knitting a scarf for the cold. Now it is gone."

Biscuit sniffed the hay. Sniff, sniff. He sniffed the fence. Sniff, sniff, sniff. He sniffed the wheelbarrow. "I smell wool!" he barked.

They followed the smell around the corner. Biscuit bumped into a bucket. CLANG! He bonked into a fence post. BONK! Then he rolled right over the yarn ball.

Uh-oh. The yarn wrapped around his legs. It wrapped around his ears. It wrapped around his tail.

"Oh dear," said Biscuit. He wobbled in a circle. Wobble, wobble, spin. "I am a yarn puppy!"

Mabel tried very hard not to laugh. Her beak wiggled. Her feathers puffed out. "Hold still, silly pup," she said. "I will help."

Mabel pecked at the loose end. Peck, peck, peck. Biscuit wiggled. Wiggle, wiggle, wiggle. Slowly, slowly, the yarn unwound. Around and around and around. At last, the puppy was free. The yarn was a fat, round ball again.

Mabel gave a happy cluck. "Thank you, Biscuit. You sniffed out my yarn."

Biscuit wagged his tail. Thump, thump, thump on the straw. "Can we play now?"

"Maybe later," said Mabel. Click, click, click went her knitting needles. Biscuit rested his chin on her warm feathers.

The sky turned pink, then gold, then soft and dim. Click... click... click. The needles slowed down. Mabel's eyes drooped.

Biscuit's tail gave one last sleepy thump. Then he began to snore. Snore-snore-rumble.

"Grumble-bumble," whispered Mabel, very softly. But this time, she was smiling.

Good night, Biscuit. Good night, barn. Good night, yellow yarn.

Shh. Good night.

He had three curly horns, two big woolly feet, and the biggest appetite for cookies in the whole valley. Whenever he smelled warm butter and sugar, his tummy went GRRR-GLUMP, GRRR-GLUMP, like a grumpy old washing machine.

Every autumn, Gorble baked cookies for the Harvest Picnic in Dimbly Vale. His favorite recipe needed one special ingredient: a spoonful of moonberry jam, which glowed a soft silver in its jar. Gorble kept the jar on the highest shelf, behind the flour, where he could see it from his rocking chair.

first_draft.text:
The old farmhouse creaked when the moon climbed over the hill, and so did Ethan's bedroom door. Creeeak. Then came a whisper from somewhere under the floorboards. Shhh-shhh-hello. Ethan pulled his quilt up to his nose and listened very hard.

"Just the house settling," said Aunt Odette the next morning, buttering her toast with a crunch. But when they went down to the cellar, two jars of raspberry jam were missing from the shelf. Ethan found sticky red fingerprints on the banister, a squelchy trail of them, leading all the way up the stairs.

"Maybe a raccoon has learned to unscrew lids," said Aunt Odette, but she didn't sound sure. Ethan didn't sound sure either. That night he tucked his flashlight under his pillow and waited. Creak, went the third stair. Whisper, went the wall. Then a soft, wobbly voice said, "Oh dear. Oh dear, oh dear."

Ethan clicked on his flashlight. Hovering beside the kitchen doorway was a ghost no taller than a broom, with a sheet that had one floppy corner and two round eyes the color of pale lemonade. He clutched a jam jar to his chest with both hands, and a drip of red ran down his sheet. "I'm Bramble," he whispered. "I'm very sorry. I only wanted a tiny taste. I'm far too shy to ask anyone for things."

Ethan had expected a monster. He had not expected someone who turned a faint shade of pink when he giggled. "You could have just knocked," Ethan said. Bramble's sheet drooped all the way to the floor. "Ghosts don't knock. We float through walls, and then people shriek and run away, and nobody ever gives us jam."

Ethan thought about this. He thought about the creaks, which were Bramble drifting over the loose third stair, and the whispers, which were Bramble practicing the word hello in case he ever needed it. "What if you left a note?" Ethan said. "Aunt Odette loves notes. If you asked properly, she might say yes."

Bramble's eyes glowed brighter. Together they wrote on the back of a seed packet, in big round letters: Dear Aunt Odette, please may I have one spoonful of jam on Sundays? Yours shyly, Bramble. They taped it to the pantry door, right beside the jam shelf, and then Ethan yawned so hugely that Bramble yawned too, with a sound like a teakettle sighing.

Next morning Aunt Odette read the note aloud, laughed until she had to wipe her eyes on her apron, and set a small jar with a silver spoon on the windowsill. "Sundays," she said, tapping the glass. "And you knock first." That Sunday, the spoon lifted gently from the sill, and a happy little squeak drifted through the kitchen like a rusty swing. Ethan decided it was the best sound he had heard all week.

That night the house was quiet. The stairs stayed still. The wind hummed a low, sleepy tune across the dark fields, and the curtains swayed like slow dancers. Ethan's eyelids grew heavy, one by one, until they closed. Somewhere below, a jar lid clicked softly, and a faint whisper floated up the stairs. Goodnight, Ethan.

Goodnight, Bramble.

It was a bouncy, breezy morning at Puddlewick Castle, and the flags flapped like happy fish. Sir Pim, the smallest knight in the land, reached for his shiny silver helmet and found only a dent in his cushion.

"Oh, bother," said Sir Pim.

In its place sat a dented copper pudding bowl. It gave a small, surprised bong.

Ember, Sir Pim's dragon friend, peeked through the window. Ember was no bigger than a wheelbarrow, with a tail that curled like a question mark. "Your helmet has gone," said Ember, "and someone has left a pudding bowl in its place."

"The Great Hobby-Horse Hop starts at noon," said Sir Pim, "and I can't hop with a bowl on my head."

So Pim tucked the bowl under his arm, and off they went. First they checked the stable, where a horse named Dumpling was snoring into a bucket of oats. Dumpling opened one eye, looked at the bowl, and yawned. No helmet.

Next they tiptoed into the kitchen. Cook Mrs. Bramble was stirring a pot of porridge, and she was not smiling. "Have you seen a copper bowl?" she asked. "With a dent in the side?"

"Here it is!" said Pim, holding it up.

Mrs. Bramble clapped her floury hands. "My best pudding bowl! I've been looking all morning." She tapped it, and it went bong. "But I haven't seen a helmet. The only shiny thing I noticed was near the garden wall, glinting like a fish."

Ember's nose twitched. "Let's go look," said Ember, and that sounded like a fine plan.

Near the garden wall, they found a trail of soft white feathers, a crumb of seed cake, and a little huffing hiss. Pim crept round the rosebushes. Ember stepped carefully, which is not easy for a dragon.

There, in a nest of straw and marigolds, sat Gwendolyn the goose. She was tall, grumpy, and very proud. Tucked underneath her was the silver helmet, and inside the helmet sat three speckled eggs, snug as buttons.

"Oh," breathed Sir Pim. "Gwendolyn, that's your nest."

Gwendolyn hissed a quiet, fussy hiss.

Pim's heart went thump, thump. He could grab the helmet and hop away, but then the eggs might tumble out. Ember's tail drooped. "We can't take the eggs," whispered Ember. "Not even a little."

Pim thought hard. He looked at his woolly scarf, the green one with yellow stripes that his grandmother had knitted. He looked at the helmet. He looked at Gwendolyn, who was looking at her eggs.

Slowly, Pim unwound the scarf and laid it in a soft, wide ring beside the nest. Gwendolyn gave it a long, suspicious sniff. Then she hopped onto the scarf, nudged each speckled egg with her beak into the warm wool, and settled down with a contented sigh.

Pim lifted the helmet, polished it on his sleeve, and gave a little bow. "Thank you, Gwendolyn," he whispered. Gwendolyn blinked one sleepy eye.

They hurried back across the courtyard. Mrs. Bramble got her bowl back and laughed until she had to sit down. Sir Pim put on his helmet, which fit perfectly with a gentle clink, and hopped into the Great Hobby-Horse Hop. He wobbled a little, and Ember cheered the loudest of all.

Sir Pim pulled his blanket up to his chin. Ember curled up at the foot of the bed, warm as a teapot.

"Goodnight, Ember," whispered Sir Pim.

"Goodnight, Pim," whispered Ember.

The lamp burned low. The castle sighed. Shhh. Goodnight.

On Sunday night, Maya lay under her quilt and listened to the clock. Tick. Tock. Tomorrow was Monday. Tomorrow was her very first day at Oakwood School.

"What if nobody wants to play with me?" she whispered to Pickle, her floppy bear. Pickle did not answer. Her tummy felt full of fluttery moths.

On Monday, Dad walked her to the gate. Maya's shoes squeaked on the shiny hall floor. The classroom smelled of crayons and warm apples. Her heart went thump, thump, thump.

"Good morning, Maya!" said Mrs. Lin. "Would you like to meet Biscuit?"

Biscuit was the class hedgehog. He had a bristly back, a pointy nose, and two bead-black eyes. He lived in a tank with a squeaky wheel and a cardboard tube.

"Hello, Biscuit," Maya whispered. Biscuit snuffled, then curled up and went back to sleep.

A boy stood by the coat hooks, holding his lunchbox with both hands. He had red cheeks and a brand-new haircut.

"Are you new too?" Maya asked.

He nodded. "I'm Theo. I don't know where anything is."

"Me neither," said Maya. "Maybe we can find out together."

At snack time, Theo's pencil rolled off the table. Maya caught it with one hand. "Thanks," Theo mumbled, and his cheeks went even redder. Maya giggled, and Theo giggled too.

Then a gasp rang out from the reading corner. "Biscuit's gone!"

The tank lid was open. The fluffy blanket was rumpled. The squeaky wheel was still.

"Snuffle, snuffle, where's Biscuit?" the class sang. Everyone began to search.

They checked under the bookshelf. They checked behind the paint buckets. They checked the coat cupboard, where only wellies and one sleepy mop lived. No hedgehog anywhere.

Maya knelt down and looked very carefully. Near the tank, she spotted a tiny trail of crumbs. It led across the carpet, past the table legs, toward the big blue recycling bin.

"Theo," she whispered. "Follow the crumbs with me?"

Theo nodded and crept beside her. Step, step, tiptoe. Snff, snff. Something rustled inside a cardboard box.

Maya peeked over the edge. There, curled in a brown paper tube, sat Biscuit, munching a cracker crumb. "Found you!" Maya whispered.

"Good spotting, Maya!" Theo grinned. The whole class cheered. Biscuit uncurled, blinked his bead eyes, and waddled right into Maya's hands. He was prickly, but he was warm.

At lunch, Maya and Theo sat side by side. Theo shared his cheese sandwich. Maya shared her grapes, one by one. Her tummy did not feel like moths anymore. It felt like a warm cup of cocoa.

That evening, the sun slid low behind the trees. Maya's backpack hung on its hook. Her shoes sat by the door, quiet and tired.

Pickle waited on her pillow, smelling of glue and apples. Maya pulled the quilt up to her chin.

"Goodnight, Biscuit," she yawned. "Goodnight, Theo."

The clock went tick. Tock. Soft. Slow.

Snuffle, snuffle, went the sleepy hedgehog, far away in the dark. Goodnight, friends.

Sam's bedroom was too quiet that week. Every night, before he fell asleep, he reached down into the blankets, hoping to feel a warm, wiggly weight pressed against his feet. Every night he found only cold sheets. Biscuit, his old brown dog with one white ear, was gone.

Sam tried to be busy. He built a tower of blocks that wobbled and fell with a clatter. He drew a picture of Biscuit chasing a leaf, but the tail came out crooked, and that made him frown. He pulled the knotted rope toy out of the drawer, gave it one squeak, and put it back quickly. His throat felt tight, like a knot in a shoelace.

Grandma Rose came in with a mug of cocoa that smelled of cinnamon. She sat on the edge of his bed and watched the steam curl upward. "I miss him too," she said. "Would you like to make a little garden corner for Biscuit, out by the fence? Somewhere we can go to remember him."

Sam nodded slowly. "Can it have flowers?"

"Lots of flowers," said Grandma. "And one very grumpy scarecrow, if you like."

The next morning, they went outside in their wellies. The grass was wet and went squish, squish under their boots. Grandma's gardening hat had a plastic daisy on the brim that bobbed every time she laughed. A robin hopped right onto the daisy and stayed there, cocking its head. "Hello, Mr. Robin," Grandma said solemnly. "Are you the new gardener?" The robin flew off with a loud chirrup, and Sam giggled so hard he nearly dropped the trowel.

They dug a neat square by the fence. The soil was dark and crumbly and smelled like rain. Sam found a fat pink worm and held it up. "Hello, Wiggles," he whispered. "Biscuit would have wanted to sniff you." Then his chin wobbled, and he sat back on his heels.

Grandma didn't say anything. She just shuffled over and rested her hand on his back. Sam let himself cry a little, and then a little more. Then he laughed at a sneeze from the daisy hat, and then he cried again. It was all mixed up, like muddy puddle water, and it was all right.

Grandma pulled a crinkly packet of seeds from her pocket. Sam pressed each one into the dirt with his thumb, carefully, one, two, three, all the way to ten. Then he went to fill the watering can at the tap. It went glug, glug, gloop, and water sloshed over his socks. He poured slowly over the seeds, the way he used to fill Biscuit's bowl. Drip, drip, drip, went the water into the soil.

That evening, the sky turned the color of peaches. Sam sat on the back step with a blanket around his shoulders. Grandma hummed a slow song. Far off, an owl called, soft and low. Hoo. Hoo.

Sam looked at the little square of dirt, dark with water and quiet in the dusk. The breeze moved gently through the grass. The light slipped down behind the fence, one warm slice at a time.

"Goodnight, Biscuit," Sam whispered.

The leaves rustled back, very softly.

first_draft.text:
High in an old oak tree lived a sleepy owl named Hazel. Her feathers were soft as dandelion fluff, and her eyes kept drooping shut.

"Hoo, hoo, the night is slow," she sang. "Hoo, hoo, it's time to go."

One evening, Hazel flew over the meadow. The round moon shone like a silver button. Then a cloud drifted by, slow as a sleepy sheep. The moon slipped behind it, and the meadow went dim.

"Oh dear," whispered Hazel. "Where is my tree?"

Down in the grass, a field mouse named Pip wiggled his whiskers. "I can help," he squeaked. "But it's too dark to see the path."

Hazel landed beside him, soft as a snowflake. "Let's listen," she said. "Listen for home."

They sat very still. Tinkle, tinkle went the brook over the pebbles. Chirp, chirp went the crickets in the reeds. Creak, creak went an old tree far away.

"That's my tree!" said Hazel. "It creaks like a rocking chair."

"Follow the water," said Pip, scampering off. "And count the thistles with me."

"One thistle, two thistles, three." Pip tapped each one with his tiny paw. "Now the big gray stone."

Hazel swooped low over the stone. Her wings went whoosh, whoosh, and the tall grass rustled softly.

Creak, creak. The oak tree stood just ahead, with its cozy hollow tucked under the branches.

Hazel hopped inside, and Pip curled up in the soft moss at the bottom of the trunk. The moss was warm and smelled like rain.

Then the cloud drifted away, and the moon peeked out again. Silver light spilled over the meadow like warm milk.

Hoo, hoo, went Hazel, soft as a whisper.

Hush, hush, said Pip, with a yawn.

The brook tinkled. The crickets hummed. Somewhere, a sleepy frog yawned too. The old oak creaked, gently, gently.

Hazel's eyes closed. Pip's whiskers stopped twitching. Goodnight, meadow. Goodnight, moon. Goodnight, sleepy owl.

first_draft.title: Zoe and the Sleepy Crystal Garden
first_draft.text:
On a bright, breezy morning, Zoe clambered up the grassy hill behind Grandma Mae's cottage. Her boots went squish, squish in the wet grass. Her pocket held a flashlight, a notebook, and a bag of raisins. At the mouth of a dark cave sat Grandma Mae on a flat rock, sipping tea from a flask. Beside her, in a patch of warm sunshine, sat Pebble, Zoe's tortoise, who was not interested in caves at all.

'Just a little way in,' said Grandma. 'Keep me in sight, and call if you need me.'

'I will,' promised Zoe, and she clicked on her flashlight.

Inside, the air was cool and smelled of rain and wet stone. Drip. Plink. Drip. Water tapped the walls like a patient friend knocking at a door. Zoe tiptoed past rocks shaped like sleeping elephants and hanging stones that looked like icicles made of honey. She ran her fingers along the wall. It felt smooth and cold, like a spoon left in the fridge.

Then she turned a corner, and the cave lit up. Zoe gasped so loudly that the echo gasped right back. Spread before her was a garden of crystals. Pink ones stood as tall as her shoulders. Purple ones curled like sleepy fern fronds. Tiny yellow ones sparkled across the floor like scattered sugar. Every crystal glowed softly and hummed a note like a spoon tapping a glass.

'Hello,' said a voice, small and polite.

Zoe looked down. Sitting on a crystal step was a sprite no taller than a teacup. She had moss for hair and a jacket made of dewdrop-green leaves. 'I am Nim,' she said, 'and I am the keeper of this garden. I sweep the dust off every crystal, every single morning.'

But today Nim's round face was worried. She pointed to the middle of the garden. There, where a great blue crystal should have glowed like a little moon, was only an empty hollow. The whole garden had dimmed, the way a room does when someone turns down the lamp.

'The Moon Crystal is missing,' Nim whispered. 'Without it, the others are getting sleepy.'

Zoe rolled up her sleeves. 'Then let's find it!'

First they checked behind the tall pink crystals. Nothing but cold stone. They peeked under a ledge where stony ferns drooped. They shone the flashlight into a narrow tunnel. Zoe cupped her hands and called, 'Hello, Moon Crystal!' Her voice bounced back, hello, hello, hello, until it sounded like a whole crowd of friends. But no blue glimmer answered.

Zoe sat down on the chilly floor to think. She thought about Pebble, who never hurried anywhere. Pebble would sit very still and look very carefully. So Zoe sat very still, and she listened.

Drip. Plink. Drip. Then came a new sound. Clink. Clink. Like a teaspoon against a teacup. It came from somewhere down a sloping path. Zoe followed it, past a bubbling stream, to a shallow pool. Under the water, a blue glint winked up at her.

'Nim,' said Zoe slowly, 'do you know how the Moon Crystal got in there?'

Nim wrung her mossy hands. 'It was me,' she said in a small voice. 'I swept too hard yesterday, and it rolled right off the step. I was scared you would be cross with me, so I hid the empty spot with a leaf and hoped nobody would notice.'

Zoe thought about that. She didn't feel like scolding. She felt a little sorry for Nim, who had been carrying a worry all by herself.

'Thank you for telling me the truth,' Zoe said. 'That was brave. Now let's fix it together.'

Zoe knelt by the pool and slid her hands into the cold water. She lifted the Moon Crystal out, and drips ran down her wrists. It was smooth and heavy and blue as a winter sky.

'Careful now,' she said, and she carried it as gently as an egg.

Nim hopped ahead, clearing the path. When they reached the garden, Zoe set the crystal into its hollow. Click! Light flowed out from the center in a ripple. First the pink crystals brightened, then the purple ones, and last of all the tiny yellow ones, twinkling like sugar in the sun. The whole garden hummed a louder, happier tune.

Nim clapped her tiny hands. Then she reached into her leaf-jacket and pulled out a sliver of crystal no bigger than a grain of rice. 'For you,' she said. 'So you can remember the garden.'

'Thank you, Nim,' said Zoe. 'I think the garden taught me something too. When something goes missing, looking carefully helps. And when you tell the truth early, the problem gets smaller and friends can help you fix it.'

Nim nodded so hard her moss hair bounced. 'Then I will sweep more gently,' she said, 'and I will tell you sooner next time.'

Zoe waved goodbye, and she walked back toward the daylight with the sliver of crystal warm in her pocket. Grandma Mae looked up from her rock and smiled. Pebble was still in the sunshine, blinking slowly at the grass.

'Did you find anything?' asked Grandma.

'A friend,' said Zoe. 'And a garden that was sleepy, but not anymore.'

Pebble blinked again, as if he understood every word.

Now the cottage is quiet. The kettle has cooled, and the stars are peeking over the hill. Pebble is tucked into his cozy box, with one lettuce leaf for a pillow. Zoe's sliver of crystal glows as soft as a nightlight on her windowsill.

Far beneath the hill, the garden hums its gentle song. The pink crystals are yawning. The purple ones are drooping. The tiny yellow ones are blinking slowly, one by one.

Goodnight, garden.

Goodnight, Nim.

Shh. Everything is sleeping now, and so can you.
